# Serving and Inference Infrastructure {#sec-serving}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements here are small on purpose —
about 150 short requests against a 3B model on a laptop, a few minutes in
total. They are enough because what matters is a ratio whose *sign and cause*
are the same on every machine — prefill is compute-bound, decode is
bandwidth-bound (limited by how fast weights can be read from memory, not by
arithmetic). The magnitude does not transfer, and the chapter says where
it stops transferring rather than pretending otherwise. Everything that needs a GPU fleet to observe is
cited rather than claimed. Every condition is measured five times and reported
as a median; the conditions are run in shuffled order, so drift cannot pile up
in the long-prompt rows; and a fixed short prompt is re-timed at intervals
through the session (11 times in all) as a control. On the run printed here that control held to **2.0%** across the
whole session, which is what makes the rest of the table worth reading.
Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `llama3.2:3b` (Q4_K_M, 28 layers, 24
attention heads, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128), `num_ctx` 8192,
`temperature` 0, `OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1` and `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0`,
on Python 3.14.5 and Apple Silicon. The exact chip matters more than that name
suggests, and the timings say which class it was: 190 decode tokens per second
against a 2.0 GB weight file is about **380 GB/s** of weight streaming, which
only a high-bandwidth part sustains. The same model on a 120 GB/s laptop tops
out near 60 tokens per second. Reproduce the ratio, not the rate.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- split a request into prefill and decode, and say which half your latency is
  actually made of;
- read the KV cache as the thing that makes generation fast and long context
  expensive, and size it in gigabytes before you rent the hardware;
- explain what batching buys the operator and what it costs the individual
  user;
- use prompt caching as the first lever, and recognise the prompt layouts that
  make it do nothing;
- build a cost-per-request worksheet from token counts you can measure today;
- order the remaining levers — smaller model, quantization, speculative
  decoding — by what each one actually trades away.

## One request, two very different halves {#sec-serving-halves}

Everything downstream of this chapter — the gateway of @sec-gateway, the
traces of @sec-observability, the bill in @sec-governance — is easier to reason
about once you can see that a single request is not one operation but two,
with different costs and different bottlenecks.

::: {#gloss-prefill-decode .column-margin .term-gloss}
**prefill / decode** — the two halves of a request: the prompt is read in one
parallel pass, then output tokens are produced one at a time, each depending
on the last. [↩](#term-prefill-decode){.term-back}
:::

[**Prefill / decode**](#gloss-prefill-decode){#term-prefill-decode .term-ref}
is the split. **Prefill** reads the prompt. Every token is available at once,
so the whole prompt goes through the network as one batched matrix
multiplication — the hardware is busy and the work is compute-bound.

**Decode** writes the answer. Token *n+1* cannot be computed until token *n*
exists, so each one is a separate pass over the whole model, and the machine
spends most of its time moving weights from memory rather than multiplying
them.

That asymmetry is the chapter's foundation, and it is easy to measure. Six
prompt lengths, each with its own text so nothing is cached, generating 32
tokens:

```text
prompt tokens   prefill   prefill tok/s      decode tok/s
           96    0.064s            1,433            191.3
          298    0.153s            2,007            192.2
          572    0.277s            2,047            190.9
        1,095    0.520s            2,104            182.9
        2,156    1.055s            2,043            177.9
        4,247    2.292s            1,848            161.2
```

Prefill runs at roughly **2,000 tokens per second**; decode at roughly **190**.
[On this hardware, prefill time per token was about eleven times lower than
decode time per token]{.hl} — on the 4,247-token row, 0.54 milliseconds against
6.2. That is a statement about *time*, not about a provider's price list, where
output tokens usually cost several times input — and it is the ratio rather
than the absolute numbers that survives a change of hardware. Take both figures
from the same row: decode slows as the context grows (5.2 ms at 96 tokens,
6.2 ms at 4,247), so pairing the best prefill with the worst decode inflates
the gap. Prefill also dips a little on the longest row, most likely for a
related reason: each prompt token attends to every token before it, so the
attention part of prefill grows faster than the prompt does.

::: {.column-margin}
The 1,433 tok/s on the first row is not a slower prefill; it is a fixed
per-request overhead that a 96-token prompt cannot amortise. Five repetitions
confirm it, and they also make it the noisiest row in the table — 34.5% spread
against 2–7% everywhere else, because the fixed cost dominates a prompt that
small. An earlier single-shot version of this table reported **105 decode
tok/s** on the last row; repeated five times it is 161, with 0.7% spread. That
is what one measurement buys you. Each column is its own median over the five
runs, so dividing one printed column by another (96 ÷ 0.064 = 1,500) can differ
a little from the printed rate.
:::

So a first, crude latency model, good enough to argue with:

$$
\text{latency} \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{prompt tokens}}{\approx 2{,}000/\mathrm{s}}}_{\text{prefill}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\text{output tokens}}{\approx 190/\mathrm{s}}}_{\text{decode}}
$$

**What we will look at.** First where the wall clock actually goes, which at
production prompt lengths is almost entirely prefill — and why streaming cannot
touch that. Then the KV cache, which is what makes decode fast and what makes a
long context expensive, in gigabytes you can compute before renting anything,
and how it adds up with the weights to the memory a card needs. Then batching, which buys the operator throughput and charges the individual
user for it. Then prompt caching, the one lever with no quality cost and the
largest measured win in this chapter. Then the cost worksheet, which is four
numbers and a multiplication. And finally the remaining levers, in the order to
reach for them rather than the order they get proposed in.

## Where the wall clock actually goes {#sec-serving-ttft}

::: {#gloss-time-to-first-token-ttft .column-margin .term-gloss}
**time to first token (TTFT)** — how long the reader waits before anything
appears: queueing, prefill and the first decode step. Prefill dominates on long
prompts; streaming does not shorten it, it makes it the wait the user feels.
[↩](#term-time-to-first-token-ttft){.term-back}
:::

Users do not experience total latency. They experience
[**time to first token (TTFT)**](#gloss-time-to-first-token-ttft){#term-time-to-first-token-ttft .term-ref}
and then a stream. Measuring it with streaming on, at four context lengths,
each generating 64 tokens:

```text
context tokens    TTFT     total    TTFT share
           90   0.132s   0.487s        27.1%
          960   0.506s   0.863s        58.7%
        3,731   2.061s   2.476s        83.2%
        7,427   4.715s   5.182s        91.0%
```

[At 7,427 tokens of context, 91% of the request is over before the first
character appears.]{.hl} The model is not "slow"; the prompt is long, and the
user is waiting on prefill.

Two consequences that get missed.

**Streaming does not fix TTFT.** It fixes everything *after* it. Streaming
converts a 5.2-second wait into a 4.7-second wait followed by text arriving at
reading speed, which is a large perceived improvement — but the 4.7 seconds is
untouched, and no amount of front-end work will touch it. The lever for TTFT
is the prompt, and @sec-serving-cache is the cheapest version of that lever.

**A long context makes decode slower too, not just prefill.** Every generated
token attends over everything before it, so the per-token cost grows with what
is already in the window. Measured separately — five repetitions, as
everywhere else, with 64 output tokens each so the rate is stable:

```text
context tokens   decode tok/s   ms per token
            83          189.1           5.29
           965          186.7           5.36
         3,731          160.6           6.23
         7,414          140.9           7.10
```

A 25% slowdown between an empty window and a 7,400-token one. Worth knowing
because it compounds: a long prompt costs you once in prefill and then again,
quietly, on every token you generate.

When you compare this table with the first one, compare at matching context
lengths. The first table's 4,247-token row (161 tok/s) agrees, within noise,
with this table's 3,731-token row (161), not with the 7,414-token one (141). A
number taken from the wrong row is still a wrong number; it just looks sourced.

Two names for what these tables measure, because dashboards use them. The
right-hand column — milliseconds per generated token — is the
**time per output token (TPOT)**, also called inter-token latency; together with
TTFT it describes what *one* user feels. **Throughput** is the other axis:
tokens per second summed over every request the server is handling at once. It
is what the operator pays for, and @sec-serving-batching shows why the two
pull against each other.

## The KV cache, and why context has a price in gigabytes {#sec-serving-kv}

Decode would be far worse than 5.2 ms per token if each step recomputed the
whole prompt. It does not, because of the
[**KV cache**](#gloss-kv-cache){#term-kv-cache .term-ref}: the keys and values
computed for every previous token are kept, so step *n+1* computes one new
column and reads the rest.

::: {#gloss-kv-cache .column-margin .term-gloss}
**KV cache** — the stored keys and values from earlier tokens, so generation
does not recompute the whole prompt at every step. Fast, and the reason long
context costs memory. [↩](#term-kv-cache){.term-back}
:::

That is a straight time-for-memory trade, and the memory is computable before
you rent anything. Per token the cache holds a key and a value, for every
layer, for every KV head:

$$
\text{bytes per token} \;=\; 2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes per element}
$$

For this model at fp16 — 28 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 — that is
$2 \times 28 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 114{,}688$ bytes, or **112 KiB
per token**. Multiply by the window:

| context | cache, fp16 | cache, q8_0 | fp16 cache vs 6.4 GB of fp16 weights | fp16 cache vs the 2.0 GB Q4 file |
|--:|--:|--:|:--|:--|
| 8,192 | 0.88 GiB | 0.46 GiB | 0.15× | 0.47× |
| 32,768 | 3.50 GiB | 1.86 GiB | 0.59× | [1.9×]{.con} |
| 131,072 | **14.00 GiB** | **7.44 GiB** | [2.3×]{.con} | [**7.5×**]{.con} |

: What the window costs in memory, llama3.2:3b
{tbl-colwidths="[14,14,14,29,29]"}

::: {.column-margin}
The fp16 columns, which the two ratio columns also use, are the default and the
right first calculation. The server these timings came from ran the q8_0 column
instead: `OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0`, an 8-bit cache at 1.0625 bytes per
element once the block scale is counted, which puts it at **59.5 KiB per
token** and 7.4 GiB at the full window — a little over half the fp16 figure. Quantizing the *cache* is a separate lever from
quantizing the weights, it is the one that moves the number that actually
binds, and it is off by default. Check which one your server is running before
you size a card, because nothing in the output tells you.
:::

[A 2.0 GB quantized model file with its 131k window full at fp16 needs 14 GiB
of cache.]{.hl} Note what that last ratio compares before quoting it: four-bit
weights against a sixteen-bit cache, which is the widest of the three honest
comparisons. At matched precision the cache is **2.3×** the weights; against
the eight-bit cache this chapter actually ran it is **4.0×** the file. All
three say the same thing — the cache is the allocation that scales with usage,
and it is the one nobody budgets for — but only one of them is the number to
size a card with, and which one depends on what you are running.

This is why "can I run a 3B model?" is the wrong
question and "at what context length?" is the right one, and why the default
`num_ctx` in a local server matters so much: ask for the full 131k window and
you have committed 14 GiB (about 15 GB) before the first request.

The 8 KV heads against 24 attention heads in that arithmetic are
**grouped-query attention**, and they are the reason the number is 14 GiB
rather than 42 — three heads share each key-value pair. It is a
memory-bandwidth optimisation that shows up as a serving cost, which is a
recurring shape: architecture choices from @sec-transformers reappear here as
line items.

**Sizing a card, all together.** The memory a server needs is roughly
*weights + KV cache per sequence × concurrent sequences + a working margin* for
activations and the runtime itself. Weights are parameters × bits per weight ÷ 8.
This model's 3.2 billion weights take 6.4 GB at 16 bits and 2.0 GB as Q4_K_M —
about five bits per weight on average, not four, because some tensors are kept
at higher precision and every small block of weights carries its own scale.
Served at fp16 with one 32k-token conversation, that is 6.4 GB of weights plus
3.5 GiB (3.8 GB) of cache, about 10 GB before the margin. Four such
conversations at once need 14 GiB of cache, and the cache is now more than
twice the weights.

For a mixture-of-experts model (@sec-moe), put the *total* parameter count into
that formula: every expert must be in memory, because any token may be routed
to any of them. The *active* count is what sets per-token speed. That is how
`qwen3.6:35b-a3b` in @sec-classification needs a 23.9 GB file yet served
documents slightly faster than the dense 9.7B model. (Under heavy batching,
different tokens pick different experts, so more of the weights are read at
every step and that speed advantage narrows.)

At fleet scale the same pressure produced **PagedAttention**, which manages the
cache in fixed-size blocks like virtual memory instead of one contiguous
reservation per request [@kwon2023pagedattention]. The waste it removes is
fragmentation — room reserved for 2,000 tokens by a request that generated
200, and the unusable gaps left between such reservations — and removing it is
what lets a server hold many more concurrent sequences on the same card.
Because blocks can be shared, it also lets several requests point at one copy
of a common prompt prefix, which is what @sec-serving-cache builds on.

## Batching: throughput the individual user cannot feel {#sec-serving-batching}

### Why decode is bandwidth-bound, and where that stops

"Decode is memory-bound" has been asserted four times by now. Here is the
derivation, because it also tells you the one thing the assertion does not: how
far batching goes before it stops being free.

A decode step for a batch of $B$ sequences does about $2NB$ floating-point
operations and moves about $N \cdot b$ bytes of weights, where $N$ is the
parameter count and $b$ the bytes per parameter. Their ratio — the **arithmetic
intensity** — is

$$I \;=\; \frac{2NB}{N b} \;=\; \frac{2B}{b}$$

and note what cancelled: the model size. Intensity depends on batch and
precision only. A chip is compute-bound above its *ridge point*, peak FLOP/s
divided by peak bandwidth — for an H100-class part, roughly
$989 \text{ TFLOP/s} \div 3.35 \text{ TB/s} \approx 295$ FLOP/byte. So at fp16
decode stays bandwidth-bound until about $B = 295$; at four-bit weights, until
about $B = 74$.

Prefill is the same formula with the prompt length in place of $B$. For the
4,247-token prompt above, at fp16, that is an intensity of 4,247 — more than an order of
magnitude past the ridge, which is exactly why prefill is compute-bound and
decode is not, and why the two halves of the table behave so differently.

That number is also the honest boundary on the claim that follows.

Decode is memory-bound: the hardware spends its time moving weights, not
multiplying them. That means a second request costs *almost nothing extra*,
because the weights being moved for one sequence can serve several at once.
Batching converts that slack into throughput — and the second request is nearly
free, and so is the fiftieth, and somewhere around the three-hundredth it is
not, because the batch has crossed the ridge and the arithmetic starts to
cost.

In practice the limit arrives sooner, for two reasons the formula leaves out.
Each sequence also reads its *own* KV cache at every step, and that traffic is
not shared across the batch, so at long context it grows with $B$ and pulls
intensity down. And every sequence's cache must fit in memory: on real cards
it is usually memory, not the ridge, that caps the batch.

::: {#gloss-continuous-batching .column-margin .term-gloss}
**continuous batching** — new requests join a running batch as slots free,
instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish. The throughput lever in
every modern server. [↩](#term-continuous-batching){.term-back}
:::

Naive batching waits for a full batch and then runs it to completion, so one
long generation holds the whole batch hostage.
[**Continuous batching**](#gloss-continuous-batching){#term-continuous-batching .term-ref}
— iteration-level scheduling, introduced by Orca [@yu2022orca] and standard
since — lets a finished sequence leave and a queued one take its slot at the
next step.

I did not measure this, and should say so plainly: a single-stream local server
is the wrong instrument, and inventing a number here would be worse than
citing one. What the literature reports is large: Orca's authors measure order-
of-magnitude throughput gains over naive batching at the same latency budget
[@yu2022orca], and vLLM reports 2–4× over the serving systems that preceded it
by combining continuous batching with paged cache management
[@kwon2023pagedattention].

The part worth internalising is the trade, not the multiple:

| | throughput | single-request latency |
|:--|:--|:--|
| No batching | [worst]{.con} | [best]{.pro} |
| Static batching | better | [worst — waits for the slowest sequence]{.con} |
| Continuous batching | [best]{.pro} | slightly worse than none, far better than static |

: What batching does to each number {tbl-colwidths="[28,24,48]"}

[Batching is a throughput optimisation that individual users pay for in
latency.]{.hl} Every request shares the machine with its batch-mates, so a
busy server is a slower server per request even when it is a cheaper server per
request. If your product has a latency SLO, it is a constraint on batch size,
and somebody has to own that number.

## Prompt caching: the lever to reach for first {#sec-serving-cache}

If prefill dominates latency and the prompt begins with the same thousands of
tokens every time — a system prompt, a tool schema, a few-shot block, a
retrieved document being asked about repeatedly — then that prefix's KV cache
can be computed once and reused.

::: {#gloss-prompt-caching .column-margin .term-gloss}
**prompt caching** — reusing the KV cache of a prompt prefix across requests,
so a repeated system prompt is not recomputed.
[↩](#term-prompt-caching){.term-back}
:::

[**Prompt caching**](#gloss-prompt-caching){#term-prompt-caching .term-ref} is
not a subtle optimisation. The same six prompts as the first table, each sent
twice:

```text
prompt tokens   cold prefill   warm prefill   speedup   cold total   warm total
           95         0.066s         0.016s        4x       0.300s       0.252s
          303         0.151s         0.016s       10x       0.386s       0.252s
          564         0.277s         0.014s       19x       0.514s       0.251s
        1,090         0.538s         0.016s       34x       0.781s       0.259s
        2,149         1.060s         0.012s       88x       1.311s       0.261s
        4,247         2.290s         0.015s      153x       2.562s       0.286s
```

Warm prefill is **flat at 12–16 milliseconds regardless of prompt length**,
because nothing is being recomputed. At 4,247 tokens that is 153× on the
prefill and **9.0× on the whole request**.

The longer the prefix, the larger the win — which is the opposite of how most
optimisations scale, and it is why this is the first thing to try.

Three conditions, and all three are design decisions rather than
configuration:

**The prefix must be byte-identical.** A timestamp, a user name, or a session
id near the top of the prompt invalidates everything after it. Cached prefixes
match by prefix, so one changing token at position 12 discards the other 4,000.

**Order the prompt by stability.** System instructions, then tool schemas, then
few-shot examples, then retrieved context, then the user's turn. Most teams
write prompts in the order they thought of them, which puts the volatile part
first and turns the cache off without anybody noticing.

**Measure the hit rate or you do not have one.** A cache you have not
instrumented is a belief. @sec-observability is where that instrumentation
belongs, and the metric is share of prompt tokens served from cache, per route.

**What was measured, and what was not.** The 153× above is a local server's
*slot-level* prefix reuse: the previous request's KV cache is still resident
and the next request happens to share its prefix. That is the same *mechanism*
a hosted API uses, but not the same *system*, and three differences change the
number you will see in production.

Eviction is the big one. `ollama` keeps one slot per model by default
(`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1`), so
a single interleaved request from another user discards the prefix — and the
measurement above sent the same prompt twice in a row, which is the friendliest
case that exists. Two users alternating would have shown nothing. Servers
built on paged blocks, such as vLLM and SGLang, keep many cached prefixes at
once and share them between requests, which softens this but does not remove
it. Control is
the second: some hosted APIs cache automatically above a minimum prefix length,
others require an explicit marker, and a local server gives you neither knob.
Price is the third: hosted cached input tokens are billed at a discount rather
than skipped, and some providers charge extra for the request that writes the
cache. That discount is the line the worksheet in @sec-serving-cost depends on.

Take 153× as an upper bound on the mechanism, and instrument the real hit rate
on the real system.

## The cost worksheet {#sec-serving-cost}

Latency was the first half of the argument. The bill is the other half, and
both are made of the same tokens — which is why the first thing to establish is
*which* tokens.

From @sec-summarization, summarizing a 300-word news article measured
**890 prompt tokens against 53 generated** — a ratio of nearly 17 to 1. That
shape is typical of anything with a system prompt, a schema and retrieved
context, which is to say most production LLM features.

[On this shape of workload, most of what you pay for is reading]{.hl}, and that
inverts the usual intuition about where to optimise. One conversion step before
you act on it: providers bill output tokens at several times input, so a 17:1
token ratio is nearer 3:1 or 4:1 in money, and a cache hit discounts the input
side further. Do the multiplication with your own price sheet. On this ratio it
survives — asking for shorter answers saves little, sending less saves a lot —
and on a task that generates more than it reads it would not.

The worksheet has four lines and one multiplication:

| line | where it comes from | example |
|:--|:--|--:|
| prompt tokens | count them; do not estimate | 890 |
| of which cached | measure the hit rate | 60% |
| output tokens | count them | 53 |
| requests per month | product, not engineering | 2,000,000 |

: Everything a cost estimate needs {tbl-colwidths="[26,44,30]"}

Multiply out with your provider's three prices — uncached input, cached input,
output — and you have a monthly bill with a cache-hit-rate term you can move.
With illustrative prices, not any provider's, of \$1.00 per million uncached
input tokens, \$0.10 per million cached and \$4.00 per million output tokens,
the example works out as:

| line | tokens per month | price per million | cost per month |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| uncached input (40% of 890) | 712 M | \$1.00 | \$712 |
| cached input (60% of 890) | 1,068 M | \$0.10 | \$107 |
| output (53) | 106 M | \$4.00 | \$424 |
| **total** | | | **\$1,243** |

: The worksheet multiplied out, at illustrative prices {tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

Without the cache the same traffic costs \$2,204, of which input is \$1,780.
Two things to read off it: the hit rate is worth more than any change on the
output side, and once the cache works, input is about two thirds of the *bill*
even though it is 94% of the *tokens*.

The widget below is that arithmetic, wired to the latency model from
@sec-serving-halves so both move together. It holds the measured rates
fixed, so it ignores the decode slowdown at long context and extrapolates
beyond the 7,400 tokens actually measured; read its long-prompt end as a lower
bound.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Latency and cost, on the numbers measured above — move the prompt, watch what happens</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof srvPrompt = Inputs.range([100, 32000], {
  value: 4000, step: 100, label: "prompt tokens"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof srvOutput = Inputs.range([16, 2000], {
  value: 200, step: 16, label: "output tokens"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof srvHit = Inputs.range([0, 1], {
  value: 0.6, step: 0.05, label: "prompt-cache hit rate"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
srvRates = ({prefill: 2025, decode: 190, warm: 0.015})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
srvCalc = {
  const uncached = srvPrompt * (1 - srvHit);
  const prefill  = uncached / srvRates.prefill + srvRates.warm;
  const decode   = srvOutput / srvRates.decode;
  return ({
    uncached,
    prefill,
    decode,
    total: prefill + decode,
    share: prefill / (prefill + decode),
    coldPrefill: srvPrompt / srvRates.prefill
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 680, height: 132, marginLeft: 96, marginBottom: 34,
  x: {label: "seconds", grid: true, domain: [0, Math.max(srvCalc.coldPrefill + srvCalc.decode, 0.5)]},
  y: {domain: ["no cache", "with cache"], label: null},
  color: {domain: ["prefill", "decode"], range: ["#1F4E79", "#B3453E"], legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX([
      {row: "no cache",   part: "prefill", t: srvCalc.coldPrefill},
      {row: "no cache",   part: "decode",  t: srvCalc.decode},
      {row: "with cache", part: "prefill", t: srvCalc.prefill},
      {row: "with cache", part: "decode",  t: srvCalc.decode}
    ], {x: "t", y: "row", fill: "part", inset: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<p style="font-size:0.88rem; color:var(--fig-muted); margin-top:0.5rem;">
  <b style="color:var(--fig-ink);">${srvCalc.total.toFixed(2)} s</b> per request
  — ${(srvCalc.share * 100).toFixed(0)}% of it prefill, and that share is what
  the reader waits through before the first character.
  ${srvHit > 0 ? html`Caching saves
  <b style="color:var(--fig-ink);">${(srvCalc.coldPrefill - srvCalc.prefill).toFixed(2)} s</b>
  by skipping ${(srvPrompt * srvHit).toLocaleString("en-US")} prompt tokens.`
  : html`With no cache the whole prompt is recomputed every time.`}
  At 2 million requests a month that is
  <b style="color:var(--fig-ink);">${((srvCalc.total * 2e6) / 3600).toLocaleString("en-US",
  {maximumFractionDigits: 0})} machine-hours</b> of serving, if requests are
  served one at a time; batching divides it.
</p>`
```
:::

## The levers, in the order to reach for them {#sec-serving-levers}

The order matters more than the list, because the cheap levers are also the
ones with no quality cost, and teams routinely start at the bottom.

| lever | what it buys | what it costs | reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Send fewer tokens** | linear on prefill and on the bill | engineering time on prompts and retrieval | [first, always]{.pro} |
| **Prompt caching** | up to 153× prefill, measured above | a prompt ordered by stability | [first, always]{.pro} |
| **Smaller model** | 3–10× on everything | quality, measurably | when the eval says it holds |
| **Quantization** | memory and bandwidth | some quality, task-dependent | when memory is the binding constraint |
| **Speculative decoding** | decode latency, primarily; cost depends on serving efficiency and pricing | a draft model to host | when *decode* is the slow half — long answers; little help when prefill dominates (details below) |
| **Continuous batching** | throughput | per-user latency | when the server is busy, not before |

: Six levers and what each one trades away {tbl-colwidths="[22,26,28,24]"}

Two deserve a sentence each, because both are widely misunderstood.

**Quantization** stores weights at reduced precision — the model measured in
this chapter is Q4_K_M, about five bits per weight on average. Because decode
reads every weight once per step, fewer bytes per weight also raise the decode
ceiling, roughly bandwidth ÷ weight bytes: that is how the opening note got
380 GB/s from 190 tokens per second on a 2.0 GB file, and the same chip would
top out near 60 tokens per second on the 6.4 GB fp16 weights. Modern post-training methods
choose *which* weights to keep precise rather than rounding uniformly: GPTQ
solves a layer-wise reconstruction problem [@frantar2023gptq], AWQ protects the
small fraction of weights that the activation distribution says matter most
[@lin2024awq]. Both report far less degradation than naive rounding, and both
are still degradation. It is a memory optimisation with a quality cost, and the
cost is task-dependent — which means it belongs in your eval suite, not in a
blog post's benchmark table.

**Speculative decoding** attacks the serial part directly. A small draft model
proposes several tokens; the large model scores them all in a single parallel
pass and a modified rejection-sampling step decides how many to keep, resampling
the first rejected position from a corrected distribution
[@leviathan2023speculative]. "Accepts the longest correct prefix" is the useful
picture, and at temperature 0 it is exactly the mechanism: keep draft tokens
while they match the large model's own greedy choice. With sampling it is only
approximately so: acceptance is stochastic, and a plausible draft token can
still be rejected. The
output distribution is provably unchanged — this is not an approximation — and
the win is in wall-clock, typically 2–3× when the draft model agrees often.
Note what it does *not* do: the large model still processes every token, and
also scores the rejected drafts, so FLOPs rise slightly rather than fall; on
per-token API pricing the bill does not fall either.
Self-hosted, cost follows GPU time and throughput, so the speedup can lower
cost per completed answer — measure it on your own serving load. What it buys
first is latency.

For the arithmetic underneath all of this at scale — how model size, batch
size and chip memory bandwidth combine to set what is achievable — Pope et al.
work it through properly [@pope2023efficiently], and @sec-pretraining's $6ND$
gives the training-side counterpart.

## Intuition checks {#sec-serving-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Four are settled by this chapter's
measurements and arithmetic — the two rates, the TTFT share, the KV cache arithmetic, and what a
cold prefill costs against a warm one — and the last two are the ones this
chapter deliberately did not measure, because a single-stream laptop is the
wrong instrument for batching and a general benchmark is the wrong instrument
for quantization.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your feature is "too slow". Where do you look first?

At the ratio of prompt tokens to output tokens, before you look at the model.

Prefill and decode run at very different rates — measured here, about 2,000
against 190 tokens per second — so a request with a long prompt and a short
answer spends nearly all its time reading. At 7,427 tokens of context, 91% of
the wall clock was over before the first character appeared.

If that is your shape, the levers are prompt length and prompt caching, and
speculative decoding in particular has limited end-to-end benefit — it speeds up decode.
A genuinely faster model does still help, because prefill is compute-bound and a
smaller model has less compute to do; what will not help is anything aimed at
the token-by-token half. If instead you are
generating thousands of tokens, the answer is the opposite one, which is why
the ratio is the first thing to measure rather than the last.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Does streaming reduce latency?

No. It reduces *perceived* latency after the first token, and changes nothing
before it.

Streaming cannot start until prefill finishes, so TTFT is identical with it and
without it. What streaming buys is that the remaining seconds are spent reading
rather than waiting — a real and large product improvement, and not a
performance one.

The give-away that a team has confused the two is a latency dashboard that
improved when streaming shipped. Neither TTFT nor total time should have
changed. If the number fell, the client is most likely now stopping the clock
at the first chunk instead of the last one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why can a 2 GB model need more than 16 GB of memory?

Because the weights are not the whole footprint. The KV cache holds a key and a
value for every token in the window, for every layer and every KV head.

For this model at fp16 — 28 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 — that is
112 KiB per token, so a 131,072-token window is 14 GiB (about 15 GB) of cache
on top of a 2.0 GB model file. Say what that ratio compares, though: four-bit weights
against a sixteen-bit cache. At matched precision the cache is 2.3× the
weights. An 8-bit cache roughly halves the cache side, which is a lever worth
knowing about and one that is off by default.

This is why the honest answer to "will it fit?" is a question about context
length, and why a local server's default window is a memory decision disguised
as a convenience setting.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your prompt cache hit rate is near zero and you cannot see why.

Something volatile is near the top of the prompt.

Prefix caches match by prefix: one differing token at position 12 invalidates
everything after it. A timestamp, a user id, a session identifier or a
freshly-shuffled few-shot block will all do it, and none of them look like a
performance bug.

The fix is to order the prompt by stability — instructions, then schemas, then
examples, then retrieved context, then the user's turn — and the check is to
send the same request twice and compare prefill times. Cold and warm should
differ by an order of magnitude or more; measured here, 2.290s against 0.015s.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Continuous batching raised throughput 3×. Did latency improve?

Almost certainly not, and it probably got slightly worse per request.

Batching exploits the fact that decode is memory-bound: several sequences can
share the weight movement that one sequence needs. That raises tokens per
second across the server while each individual sequence advances no faster —
and it now shares the machine.

So the two numbers move in opposite directions, and reporting only the one that
improved is a common way to mislead a review. If you have a latency SLO, it is
a ceiling on batch size, and somebody must own it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When is quantization the wrong answer?

When memory is not your binding constraint, or when nobody has evaluated it on
your task.

Quantization trades quality for memory and bandwidth. Modern methods lose much
less than naive rounding — GPTQ and AWQ both choose which weights to protect
rather than scaling everything uniformly — but "much less" is not "none", and
the loss is task-dependent in ways a general benchmark will not tell you.

If your constraint is prompt length, weight quantization does not shrink the
problem: the KV cache is a separate allocation with its own lever (the 8-bit
cache above), although memory freed from the weights can hold more cache.
Reach for weight quantization when the model
does not fit, and put it through the same eval you would use for a model swap.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-serving-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the machine

**Q: Walk me through what happens when a request hits an LLM server.**

Two phases with different characteristics. Prefill reads the whole prompt in
one parallel, compute-bound pass. Decode produces output tokens one at a time,
each a separate memory-bound pass over the model, reusing the KV cache so
earlier tokens are not recomputed. Name the rate difference — about eleven to
one per token in this chapter's measurements — and say which half dominates for
the request shape you are being asked about. Candidates who describe one
undifferentiated "inference" have not looked.

**Q: Why is the KV cache the thing that limits concurrency?**

Because it grows with tokens times sequences, while the weights are a fixed
cost. Weights are
loaded once and shared by every request on the card; the cache is per-sequence
and grows with every prompt and generated token. Give the arithmetic —
$2 \times L \times H_{kv} \times d_{\text{head}}$ values per token, times the
bytes per value — and note that
grouped-query attention exists largely to shrink it. PagedAttention is the
systems answer: manage it in blocks so a sequence that reserved 2,000 tokens
and used 200 does not waste the rest.

**Q: Where does batching help and where does it hurt?**

It helps throughput because decode is memory-bound and the weight movement is
shared. It hurts per-request latency because each sequence now shares the
machine. Continuous batching removes the worst version of the trade — the
head-of-line blocking in static batching — but does not remove the trade
itself. A candidate who says batching is free has not run a latency SLO.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: The bill doubled last month and traffic did not. Debug it.**

Input tokens first, because they dominate: 890 against 53 in this book's
summarization measurement. Look for a prompt that grew — a retrieval step
returning more chunks, a system prompt that gained a section, a conversation
history that stopped being truncated. Then the cache hit rate, because a
volatile token moved to the top of the prompt turns caching off silently and
looks exactly like a price change. Only then model or provider changes.

**Q: How would you cut latency in half without changing the model?**

Establish the split first — if it is 90% prefill, output-side changes cannot
get you there. Then: prompt caching for the stable prefix, which measured 153×
on prefill here; shortening the prompt itself, which is linear; and streaming
to convert the remaining wait into reading time. Say what you would measure
after each one, and say that speculative decoding is on the list only if you can host a draft model,
and that what it buys is decode latency — whether it also lowers cost depends on
how you pay for compute.

**Q: We want a 99th-percentile latency SLO. What do you need?**

A batch-size ceiling, an admission policy for what happens when the queue is
long, a separate route for long-context requests so they cannot sit in front of
short ones, and per-route TTFT instrumentation rather than a single global
number. Then say the uncomfortable part: a p99 SLO and maximum throughput are
in direct conflict, and somebody has to be told which one they are buying.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-serving-tools}

About 150 requests against a 3B model on a laptop — 130 timed calls across 20
conditions, each repeated five times (the cache condition sends a cold and a
warm call per repeat), plus 11 canary (control) calls and 2 discarded
warm-ups — needs exactly two things, listed in the first table below. The
second table is what you would actually serve on. None of it was used here:
the numbers in this chapter are ratios, and ratios are the part that survives
the move to a real card.

| library | version used | what it is for here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `ollama` | 0.24.0 | the local server; its `/api/generate` reports the prefill and decode split per request, which is what made these measurements cheap |
| `llama3.2:3b` | Q4_K_M | the model under test; small enough to measure on a laptop without thermal throttling |

: The stack these numbers came from. Python 3.14.5, Apple Silicon
{tbl-colwidths="[24,16,60]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| project | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `vllm` | 0.28.0 | the reference open-source server: continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching [@kwon2023pagedattention] |
| `sglang` | 0.5.18 | a serving runtime built around structured programs and aggressive prefix reuse |
| `text-generation-inference` | 3.3.7 | Hugging Face's server, closest to their ecosystem; now in maintenance mode, and Hugging Face itself recommends vLLM or SGLang for new deployments |
| `llama.cpp` | b10690 (rolling) | CPU and Apple Silicon inference; the engine `ollama` was built on (newer `ollama` versions also run many models on their own engine over the same `ggml` library). Tagged per build, so pin one |
| `tensorrt-llm` | 1.2.1 | NVIDIA's compiler-based runtime when the last 20% of throughput matters |
| `llmcompressor` | 0.13.0 | applying GPTQ and AWQ quantization [@frantar2023gptq; @lin2024awq] to a model you intend to serve |

## Lab: measure your own two halves {#sec-serving-lab}

Any local server that reports timings will do; the point is to produce your
numbers rather than to reuse mine.

### Step 1 — get the prefill and decode rates for your model

Six prompt lengths, each with distinct text so nothing caches, a fixed short
output. Record prompt tokens, prefill seconds, output tokens, decode seconds.
Two rates fall out, and their ratio is the number to remember.

### Step 2 — find your TTFT curve

Turn streaming on and record time to the first token at three context lengths.
Plot TTFT as a share of total. If it does not rise steeply, your prompts are
shorter than most production prompts and you should retest with a realistic
one.

### Step 3 — measure your cache, then break it

Send the same long prompt twice and record both. Then send it twice more with a
*fresh* timestamp at the *top* of the prompt on each call — the same timestamp
twice would still cache. The second pair should lose the speedup entirely. Keep both numbers; the difference is what prompt ordering is
worth.

### Step 4 — size the KV cache in gigabytes

Get layers, KV heads and head dimension from your model's metadata and compute
bytes per token. Multiply by the context length you were about to configure.
If the answer surprises you, that is the point of the step.

### Step 5 — build the worksheet

Prompt tokens, cached share, output tokens, requests per month, three prices.
Produce a monthly figure, then compute what a 50% prompt reduction and a 60%
cache hit rate each save. Rank them.

### Step 6 — argue for one change

One paragraph naming the single lever you would pull first, with the number
from step 5 that justifies it and the quality risk you are accepting.

### What to hand in

Your two rates and their ratio; the TTFT share at your realistic context
length; the cached and uncached prefill for the same prompt; the KV cache size
for your configured window; and the paragraph from step 6.

## Exercises {#sec-serving-exercises}

1. **Your two rates.** Measure prefill and decode tokens per second for a model
   you can run. Report the ratio and predict, before measuring, the total
   latency for a 4,000-token prompt with a 100-token answer. Then measure it.

2. **Break the cache on purpose.** Take a prompt with a long stable prefix and
   measure cold and warm prefill. Move a timestamp from the bottom of the prompt
   to the top and repeat. Report both numbers and the design rule you would
   write for your team.

3. **Size a window.** For three models you might deploy, compute KV cache bytes
   per token from their metadata and produce a table of memory against context
   length. Say which model you would run at 32k context on a 24 GB card.

4. **The worksheet, honestly.** Take a feature you have actually shipped or
   specified. Count real prompt and output tokens — count, do not estimate —
   and compute the monthly bill at your traffic. Then compute it again with the
   prompt 40% shorter, and say which parts of the prompt you would cut.

5. **TTFT against context.** Plot time to first token against prompt length for
   your setup, over at least five lengths. Fit a line. Use the slope to predict
   TTFT at a context length you have not tested, then test it.

6. **The output-length myth.** Find a place where someone proposed saving money
   by asking the model for shorter answers. Using the input/output ratio you
   measured, compute what that change would actually have saved.

## What to remember {#sec-serving-summary}

- **A request is two operations, not one.** Prefill reads the prompt in one
  parallel pass; decode writes the answer one serial token at a time. Measured
  here at roughly **2,000 against 190 tokens per second** — writing a token
  takes about **eleven times** as long as reading one. Every serving decision
  follows from which half your requests are made of.

- **Latency is usually the prompt.** At 7,427 tokens of context, **91.0% of the
  wall clock was over before the first character appeared**. Streaming does not
  change that number; it only makes the rest of the request visible. The lever
  for time-to-first-token is prompt length, and after that, caching.

- **Long context is charged twice.** It costs prefill once, and then slows every
  generated token: decode fell from **189 to 141 tokens per second** between an
  empty window and a 7,400-token one.

- **The KV cache can dwarf the model.** At 112 KiB per token, a 131k window is
  **14 GiB of cache** — 7.5× a 2.0 GB four-bit file, 2.3× the same weights at
  fp16, 4.0× the file with the eight-bit cache actually used here. Quote
  whichever matches your setup, but "will it fit?" is a question about context
  length either way. Grouped-query attention is why the number is 14 and
  not 42. Size a card as weights + cache × concurrent sequences + a margin,
  and for a mixture-of-experts model count the total parameters, not the
  active ones.

- **Prompt caching is the first lever and it is not subtle.** Warm prefill was
  **flat at 12–16 ms regardless of prompt length**: 153× on prefill and 9.0× on
  the whole request at 4,247 tokens. It requires a byte-identical prefix, so
  order the prompt by stability and put nothing volatile near the top.

- **Batching buys throughput and spends latency.** Decode is memory-bound, so
  sequences can share weight movement; continuous batching keeps the slots full
  instead of waiting for the slowest sequence [@yu2022orca;
  @kwon2023pagedattention]. Reporting the throughput gain without the latency
  cost is how a review gets misled.

- **Most of what you pay for is reading.** 890 prompt tokens against 53
  generated in this book's own summarization measurement — a token ratio, which
  becomes nearer 3:1 or 4:1 once output tokens are priced higher. Asking for
  shorter answers saves little; sending less saves a lot. Boilerplate removal
  beats model selection, and it is the one form of "send less" with no quality
  risk — dropping retrieved context or few-shot examples is a quality decision
  and belongs in the eval.

- **Order the levers by what they cost you.** Removing genuinely redundant
  tokens and reusing a cached prefix carry no quality risk and go first;
  dropping context the model uses is a quality decision. A smaller model, quantization
  [@frantar2023gptq; @lin2024awq] and speculative decoding
  [@leviathan2023speculative] each trade something specific — quality, quality,
  and a hosted draft model for latency respectively — and belong in an eval, not in a
  benchmark table someone else ran.
